title: Peter and Paul in Rome
hookLine: after Nero's fire, tradition says Peter was crucified upside down and Paul beheaded

cards: The book of Acts stops in a strange place.
Paul has reached Rome as a prisoner, after a storm and a shipwreck, and the last lines say: "And Paul dwelt two whole years in his own hired house, and received all that came in unto him."
He is teaching, "no man forbidding him." And the book ends. No verdict.
No execution. Peter dropped out of the story long before. For what happened next to both men, the churches turned to tradition, and in that tradition the story runs through a fire.

teach.b: The Roman historian Tacitus writes that after a great fire burned through Rome, the emperor Nero blamed the Christians and had them put to death in cruel ways.
Tradition places Peter and Paul in Rome in those years, and remembers their deaths. Peter, it says, was crucified, and asked to be crucified upside down, feeling unworthy to die the way his Lord had.
Paul, a Roman citizen, was beheaded with the sword. The New Testament tells neither death, but it leaves two signs.

In John's Gospel, the risen Jesus tells Peter, who had denied him by the fire: "when thou shalt be old, thou shalt stretch forth thy hands, and another shall gird thee, and carry thee whither thou wouldest not."
John adds: "This spake he, signifying by what death he should glorify God." Then: "Follow me." The man who once said "I know not the man" is told he'll follow all the way.

The second sign is a letter in Paul's name, written from prison to Timothy: "I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith."
Two very different men: the fisherman who sank in the water and the tentmaker who once made havoc of the church. They argued once, in Antioch, face to face.
Tradition remembers them together, buried in the same city, honored on the same feast, and Catholic tradition places Peter's grave beneath the church that bears his name in Rome.
Whatever you make of the traditions, both stories come to the same place: faithful to the end.

how: Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches keep a shared feast of Saints Peter and Paul, and pilgrims visit the churches in Rome built over the places tradition names as their graves.

games.q: you're Peter, old now, in Rome. tradition says you're sentenced to be crucified like your Lord. what do you ask?
games.why: tradition says he asked to be crucified upside down, unworthy to die the way Jesus did. the New Testament itself doesn't tell the story.

practice: Bring to mind one person, from any time or faith or none, who refused to say what they didn't believe and lost something for it: a job, their freedom, their life. Hold their name, what it cost, and what they kept.
If you pray, give thanks to God for them; if you don't, simply honor them in silence.
